messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mikaere, a 71-year-old Māori painter who lived alone and still took occasional commissions in a small studio attached to his home, described his distress as beginning with the bombing that tore through the public market where he had been buying supplies years earlier. He had been standing near the fruit stalls when the blast hit, and what remained most vivid for him was not an abstract fear but the exact way his body had been thrown and pinned, the dust in his mouth, the ringing in his ears, and the sight of people scrambling through smoke. Even now, when the memory forced its way into his mind without warning, it arrived with extraordinary clarity and detail; he could see the broken awning, smell the burning, and feel himself folded into the same position he had been in on the ground. At those moments, he said, it was as if his body were back there, trapped in the same posture, and the intensity of that bodily reenactment left him shaken for hours.

Over time, those intrusions came to mean something dangerous to him. Mikaere had come to believe that the memory could seize him anywhere and that, if it could do that, then he could not rely on himself to stay steady when it mattered. He spoke with the weary certainty of a man who had tried to reason his way through fear and lost confidence in his own judgment. The same experience also made other people feel unreliable; during the aftermath of the attack, he had seen how quickly a normal day could turn chaotic, and he now felt that he could not rely on other people to keep him safe either. From there, the world itself seemed less like a place he moved through and more like a place waiting to turn on him. He began to talk about the world as dangerous in an almost matter-of-fact way, as if that were simply the lesson the bombing had taught him.

Those beliefs shaped the way he lived. Mikaere started asking for reassurance more and more, phoning his sister after small outings to check that he had sounded all right, and sometimes calling a neighbor just to hear someone say he was okay. He tried hard to control his emotions in public, keeping his face still and his voice measured because he feared that if he let himself show too much, he would lose control and confirm his own sense that he could not rely on himself. Going out became something he approached cautiously and then began to avoid whenever possible. The local market, the bus stop near his apartment, even the walk to buy paint supplies could feel like places where danger might suddenly reappear, and in his small painting business that meant turning down work that required him to travel farther from home or meet clients in busy places. His world narrowed around the studio and the rooms he could manage without too much strain.

At the same time, these protective habits seemed to keep the event alive. Because he avoided going out, he had fewer ordinary experiences to interrupt the sense of threat, and the longer he stayed home, the more the bombing stayed central in his mind. When he tried to contain his feelings and push through alone, the effort left him tense and watchful, which made the memories more likely to break through; once they did, the vividness of them and the bodily feeling that accompanied them fed right back into his conviction that he was not capable of managing what happened inside him. The more he sought reassurance, the more he noticed how much he needed it, and that only deepened his belief that he could not trust himself or count on others to notice when he was slipping. In recent months this pattern had become hard to ignore: he would spend an afternoon trying not to think about the bombing, only to find the scene arrive in full detail that night, with his body seeming to lock into the old position again.

Mikaere came for help now because the circle had started to take more from his life than he could comfortably hide. He was tired of living around the edges of fear, and he had begun to worry that his shrinking routine would eventually leave him isolated from his sister, his neighbors, and the work that still gave him purpose. What frightened him most was the feeling that another reminder could send him straight back into that moment on the ground and prove, again, that he could not trust himself to come out of it. What he hoped for was not to forget the bombing, but to feel safe enough in his own body and in the ordinary world to step outside without needing someone else to tell him he was all right.
